passage: In a Cape Town park, Vera called, "Amara, come to me!" in a bright sing-song, and Amara toddled back, laughing. Then at the pond's edge Vera's voice flattened: "Amara. Stop." Amara froze, one foot in the air, and looked up at Vera's face. At the slide, Nico's minder said "Nico" in a bored voice, and Nico climbed on. A baby in a pram watched them all.

qa.q: What did Vera say at the pond's edge?
qa.a: Vera said, "Amara. Stop."

qa.q: How does Amara seem to feel when Vera's voice flattens at the pond?
qa.a: Amara seems startled and unsure, freezing mid-step and looking up at Vera's face to read the flat tone.

qa.q: What could Vera do to keep Amara safe near the pond without frightening Amara?
qa.a: Vera could walk over, crouch down and use a warm but firm voice, so the signal is clear without being alarming.

qa.q: What might the bored tone mean for Nico, who kept climbing?
qa.a: A bored tone carries little urgency, so Nico feels free to go on; the same word from a different face gave a very different signal.

grounding: A toddler stops or goes on according to a caregiver's face and tone, obeying the emotional signal more than the words.

passage: From my balcony I watch the courtyard most evenings. Hansa, about two, was touching the gate latch while her father Nilesh chatted with two other parents. He said "No, Hansa" laughing, and she grinned and touched it again. A minute later he said the same words in a flat, firm voice without turning round, and she snatched her hand away and stood still, lip trembling. I cannot say what she understood. Nilesh lifted her and rubbed her back.

qa.q: What did Nilesh say when Hansa touched the latch?
qa.a: Nilesh said "No, Hansa" laughing, and later said the same words in a flat, firm voice.

qa.q: What might Hansa be feeling when the flat voice comes and her lip trembles?
qa.a: Hansa may feel startled or worried; the trembling lip suggests a reaction to the tone, though the neighbour cannot be sure what Hansa understood.

qa.q: What could Nilesh try next time when Hansa touches the latch?
qa.a: Nilesh could walk over, take Hansa's hand and speak in the same calm voice as the first time, so tone and words match.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have meant by the second "No, Hansa" said without turning round?
qa.a: Nilesh may have been worried about little fingers at the latch, or busy talking, and not noticed the tone had changed; the neighbour cannot tell.

grounding: A toddler responds to a caregiver's tone rather than words, seen by an observer who cannot be sure of the child's inner state.

passage:
In the colony park, Sharmila toddled towards the pigeons by the fountain. “No, no, Sharmi,” her papa Amandeep sang, smiling. She saw the smile and kept going, giggling. Her grandmother on the bench laughed.
Then a scooter turned into the path. Amandeep's face changed. “Sharmila. Stop.” His voice was low and firm.
She stopped mid-step, staring at his face. Her lip trembled. He scooped her up. “Good stopping,” he said softly.

qa.q: Where were the pigeons?
qa.a: The pigeons were by the fountain in the colony park.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she stopped mid-step?
qa.a: She seemed startled and a little scared by her papa's serious face and low voice, and her lip trembled.

qa.q: How did Amandeep comfort Sharmila after she stopped?
qa.a: He picked her up, praised her softly and let her cuddle, so she felt safe again after the sharp moment.

qa.q: How might Sharmila's grandmother have seen the first "no, no"?
qa.a: She laughed, so she saw it as a playful game, just as Sharmila did, because the words came with a smile.

grounding: Shows a toddler who ignores a smiling no but stops at her father's serious face and tone, obeying the feeling more than the words.

passage:
“Ramesh, no,” Irawati laughed as he pulled a book off the shelf.
Ramesh grinned and pulled two more.
“You're laughing,” said Dadaji from the sofa. “He thinks it's a game.”
Irawati made her face serious. “Ramesh. No.”
Ramesh froze. He looked at her eyes, then back at the book.
“See?” said Dadaji. “Same word. Different mummy.”
Ramesh put the book down and crawled into her lap. “Thank you, baba,” Irawati said. “Let's put them back together.”

qa.q: What was Ramesh pulling off the shelf?
qa.a: He was pulling books off the shelf.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when he froze and looked at her eyes?
qa.a: He seemed unsure and a little anxious, checking his mummy's serious face to work out if she was upset.

qa.q: What worked to stop the book-pulling, and what came after?
qa.a: A serious face and calm tone worked where laughing didn't, and then Irawati comforted him and invited him to put the books back together.

qa.q: How does Dadaji see what happened?
qa.a: Dadaji sees clearly that Ramesh follows the tone, not the word; he says it was the same word but a different mummy.

grounding: Shows a toddler who keeps going when his mother laughs but stops at her serious face and tone, obeying the feeling over the word.

passage:
Daycare note, water play, Tuesday.
At stopping time my colleague sang, “All done, splashers!” Irawati kept splashing, laughing. Joseph watched her and splashed too.
I knelt and said quietly, “Joseph, hands out now,” my face calm, not smiling. Joseph looked at me for a long second, then held his hands up to be dried. Irawati stopped too.
Joseph reads faces before words. I'll keep a still face for safety moments and the sing-song for fun.

qa.q: What did the colleague sing?
qa.a: The colleague sang, "All done, splashers!"

qa.q: What might Joseph have been feeling when he looked up for a long second?
qa.a: Joseph was probably unsure and watchful, checking the carer's calm, unsmiling face to decide whether this was serious.

qa.q: What plan does the note-writer make, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: They plan to use a calm, still face for safety moments and the sing-song for fun, because Joseph follows faces and tone more than words.

qa.q: How did Irawati's behaviour change during the scene?
qa.a: At first Irawati kept splashing and laughing at the bright song, but after seeing Joseph stop, Irawati stopped too.

grounding: Shows a toddler who keeps playing at a sing-song voice but stops at a calm, serious face, obeying the emotional signal more than the words.

passage:
In the courtyard, two-year-old Tanuja toddled toward the buffalo's water trough. Amma called, "No, no, Tanu!" but she was laughing, so Tanuja kept going and splashed.
Then Irfan, the neighbour, set a kettle of hot tea on the low step. Amma's face went still. "Tanu. Come here," she said quietly.
Tanuja stopped, stared at Amma's face, and walked straight back to her lap. The older cousins stopped giggling too.

qa.q: What did Irfan set on the low step?
qa.a: Irfan set a kettle of hot tea on the low step.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja stop the second time, even though Amma spoke quietly?
qa.a: Amma's still face and serious tone made Tanuja feel unsure and a little worried, so the feeling behind the words mattered more than the words.

qa.q: What could Amma do so her words and face match next time?
qa.a: When something really matters, Amma could say "no" with a calm, serious face from the start instead of laughing.

qa.q: What is it like for Amma to see Tanuja ignore "No, no" but obey a quiet call?
qa.a: Amma may feel relieved, and may also notice that her laughing "No, no" told Tanuja it was a game.

grounding: Shows a toddler stopping or carrying on according to the caregiver's face and tone rather than the words.
